subject: Copywriting
title: Choice Overload Paralysis
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Choice Overload Paralysis.

hook.text: Sheena Iyengar's jam study: 24 flavors attracted crowds but sold 3%. Six flavors attracted fewer but sold 30%.

buildup.text: Too many options paralyze decision-making. Copy that presents 3 clear choices outsells pages with 20.

discovery.text: Apple's product page: one product, one hero shot, one CTA. Simplicity isn't lazy—it's strategic.

twist.text: Paradoxically, people SAY they want more options. But when given them, they buy less. Surveys lie; behavior reveals.

climax.text: The copywriter's job isn't just to persuade. It's to simplify. Remove choices to increase conversions.

punchline.text: Fewer choices, more sales. Simplicity converts.

quiz.question: What happened in Iyengar's jam study with fewer choices?

details.summary: Too many choices paralyze decision-making. The famous jam study showed that 24 options attracted more browsers but produced far fewer buyers than 6 options. In copy, simplifying choices — limiting options, highlighting recommendations — dramatically improves conversion rates.
details.whyItMatters: Modern consumers face overwhelming choice in every category. Copywriters who reduce decision complexity turn browsers into buyers by removing the cognitive burden that prevents action.
takeaways: More options attract attention but fewer options drive decisions
Decision fatigue increases with every additional choice presented
Curated recommendations reduce paralysis and increase conversions

faq.question: What is the ideal number of choices to present?
faq.answer: Research suggests three to five options is the sweet spot for most purchase decisions. One option feels like a take-it-or-leave-it demand. Two feels like a dilemma. Three to five provides a sense of control without creating paralysis.

faq.question: How can copy reduce choice overload?
faq.answer: Use 'recommended' or 'most popular' labels to highlight one option. Organize options into clear categories. Present the most important decision first and defer secondary choices. Progressive disclosure — revealing options gradually — prevents overwhelming the reader.
